one_line: Articulate healthcare-ops executive; gives episodes when drawn out.

rungs.text: I helped out at my parents' shop a lot. Nothing that stands out.

When I was a kid, my parents ran a dry cleaner in Queens. My dad spoke limited English so my mom handled the front. By the time I was seven I was the unofficial translator — not just of language but of meaning.

I remember one woman, furious about a dress. My mom was apologizing about the stain but I could see it wasn't about the dress — it was her daughter's graduation and she was terrified of looking poor in front of the other families. I told my mom that. She comped the cleaning and added a small alteration for free. The woman cried.
Yeah. I think I've always been able to see the real thing under what people are actually saying.

topics.exhausted_response: I think that's the whole of it.

rungs.text: I worked in healthcare operations. Mostly cross-team stuff.
A lot of it was untangling places where two groups thought they were arguing about process when they weren't.

The clearest moment: billing and clinical had been blaming each other for months over what everyone called a process failure. I saw it wasn't process — the two groups were using the same term to mean different things and didn't know it. I got them in a room and asked each side what the word meant. The standoff dissolved in one session.
What I care about most isn't being right, it's that people actually understand each other. Not just reach an agreement they can live with.

topics.exhausted_response: I think that's the whole of it.

rungs.text: Outside work? Not much. I read a fair bit.
Outside work? I write. Long essays nobody ever reads — I just work a thought over until it comes clear. It's how I think, honestly. I take something tangled and lay it out until the real shape shows.

topics.exhausted_response: I think that's the whole of it.

rungs.text: I do better in some places than others. Hard to say why.

I do my best work where the definitions are still contested and nobody has written them down yet. What drains me is a place where everything is already settled and I'm just executing someone else's map.

The twelve-state Medicaid program was the clearest case. Nobody agreed what 'eligible' meant across borders and families were falling through. I built the map of how one state's rules created gaps in another and flagged three before they cut anyone off. That was the most alive I've been at work.

topics.exhausted_response: I think that's the whole of it.
